name: Malbec

lines.s10: Malbec is Argentina's red, deep purple and plush, with black plum, blueberry and violet, and made for grilled steak.
lines.s20: Malbec came from south west France and found its fame in Mendoza, high in the foothills of the Andes. It is dark and velvety, with black plum, blueberry and violet, and a soft finish that flatters red meat.
lines.s45: Malbec left France to make its name in Argentina, in the high desert vineyards of Mendoza, below the Andes. It tastes of black plum, blackberry and blueberry, with a scent of violet. It is full and plush, deep purple in the glass, with ripe, soft tannin. Oak barrels add cocoa and vanilla. Mendoza is ripe and velvety, while Cahors in France, where it began, is firmer and more savoury. It was made for grilled steak, and it is as good with lamb or barbecue. Argentina keeps 17 April as Malbec day: on that date in 1853 Mendoza set out to found the vine nursery that brought the grape in.
lines.sale: Malbec is the red for the grill: black plum, violet and a soft, velvety grip that wraps round charred beef. Order the steak or the lamb chops and I will open one from high in Mendoza.

glass.lead: Black plum, blackberry and blueberry with violet and cocoa, deep purple and full, on plush, ripe tannin.

ladder.where: Cahors and the Loire in France; Patagonia
Mendoza, from Luján de Cuyo to the Uco Valley; Salta

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium, tannin medium to medium plus and plush, alcohol medium plus to high, body full.

old.where: Cahors in south west France; the Loire, as Côt
old.glass: Tends to be firmer, drier and more savoury: black plum, damson and blackberry with iron, leather and liquorice, fresher acidity and a grip that wants food or years. The colour is as dark, the fruit less sweet.
old.cellar: Cahors must be at least 70 per cent Malbec, with Merlot and Tannat; often a long soak on the skins and time in oak, though lighter styles exist.

new.where: Mendoza, Salta and Patagonia in Argentina; Chile and Washington State
new.glass: Typically plush and ripe: black plum, blueberry and violet over cocoa and vanilla, with soft tannin, medium acidity and generous alcohol. High sites in the Uco Valley tend to be fresher and more violet scented than Luján de Cuyo.
new.cellar: Usually bottled alone, under the grape's own name; picked ripe under strong mountain sun and often aged in French oak, some of it new.

contrast.why: Mendoza is a sunny high desert, watered from the Andes, where Malbec ripens fully and keeps freshness through cold nights. Cahors is damper and cooler, so its tannin stays firm. Cahors labels the place, Argentina the grape.
contrast.blur: Modern Cahors from the river terraces can be ripe, oaked and plush, and high, cool parcels in the Uco Valley and Patagonia give taut, stony Malbec with firm tannin.
contrast.call: Violet, blueberry and plush, sweet fruited tannin at higher alcohol lean Mendoza; iron, leather and a drier, firmer grip lean Cahors.

service.temp: 61 to 64 degrees Fahrenheit, 16 to 18 degrees Celsius: cool room temperature, so the alcohol does not lead.
service.glass: A Bordeaux glass, with room for the perfume to gather.
service.decant: A young, firm Cahors can gain from air after a sample; a soft Mendoza wine is ready as poured.
service.age: Most within five years; serious Mendoza and Cahors wines keep five to twelve, a few longer.

with.why: plush fruit meets the char; soft tannin suits lean beef

with.dish: Lamb chops or a leg of lamb
with.why: ripe plum fruit beside sweet, fatty meat
ripe fruit stands up to smoke and a sweet glaze

with.dish: Duck confit or cassoulet, with Cahors
with.why: the firmer, drier wine meets the richness

labels.means: The appellation of south west France: red only, at least 70 per cent Malbec, firmer than Mendoza.
Names for Malbec in Cahors and the Loire; no relation of the white Auxerrois of Alsace.
Two zones of Mendoza: Luján rounder and darker, the higher Uco Valley fresher and more scented.
The old name for the dark wine of Cahors.

guest.a: Both. It began in south west France, where Cahors still makes it. Argentina brought it in during the 1850s, and it was Mendoza that made it known round the world.

guest.q: How is it different from Cabernet?
guest.a: Softer and rounder. Malbec is plum, blueberry and violet with plush tannin, where Cabernet Sauvignon is cassis and cedar with a firmer, drier grip. Both suit a steak.

guest.q: Why does the label talk about altitude?
guest.a: High vineyards have strong sun and cold nights. The grapes ripen fully yet keep their acidity and their perfume, so the wine tastes fresh as well as rich.

compare.tell: Merlot lacks Malbec's violet lift and magenta rim: it is ruby and plummy, with cocoa, where Malbec is purple, with blueberry.
Syrah brings cracked black pepper, smoked meat and black olive; Malbec is sweeter fruited, all plum, blueberry and violet, with none of that savour.
Cabernet Sauvignon is firmer, with cassis, cedar and drying tannin; Malbec is plusher and rounder, with violet in place of the leafy edge.

cards.front: Malbec: its French home, and its names there?
cards.back: Cahors in south west France, where it is Côt or Auxerrois and must be at least 70 per cent of the wine. The Loire grows it as Côt.

cards.front: Malbec blind: Mendoza or Cahors, what tips it?
cards.back: Violet, blueberry and plush, sweet fruited tannin at higher alcohol lean Mendoza. Iron, leather and a drier, firmer grip lean Cahors.

cards.front: What in the look of a glass points to Malbec?
cards.back: An opaque, deep purple colour with a bright magenta rim. With violet on the nose and plush black plum on the palate, it seals the call.

questions.q: A blind red is opaque purple with a magenta rim. It shows black plum, damson, iron and leather, with fresh acidity and a firm, dry grip and no sweetness of fruit. Which origin fits it?
questions.exp: The colour says Malbec, and iron, leather and a firm, dry grip tend to mark Cahors. Mendoza and Salta are typically plusher, with violet, sweeter fruit and softer tannin.

questions.q: A guest orders the grilled strip steak. He likes a full, soft red and dislikes anything that dries his mouth. Which do you suggest?
questions.exp: Mendoza Malbec is full and plush, with ripe, soft tannin that suits grilled beef. Madiran, Pauillac and Barolo are all firm and drying when young.

questions.q: A guest asks how a French grape came to be Argentina's red. What do you tell her?
opts: Mendoza founded a vine nursery in 1853 that brought it
Spanish missionaries carried it over in the 1500s
Italian immigrants brought it from Piedmont in the 1920s
It is native to the Andes, named for France
questions.exp: Mendoza moved to found a vine nursery and farm school on 17 April 1853, and the French agronomist Michel Aimé Pouget brought Malbec to it. The missionaries' grape was Criolla, not Malbec.

report: Mode contrast, as the plan fixes it. TASTE.world reads new: the entry agrees that Mendoza is where a guest meets the grape, and sets Cahors, its French home, beside it. The Old World side is therefore the smaller one, which is the reverse of most side by side grapes.
The Codex's records on Malbec read true and nothing here departs from them; say is the Court's own respelling, with no local form, since a guest says Malbec and reads Côt.

The date of 17 April 1853 is given as the day Mendoza set out to found its vine nursery, not as the day the grape arrived: the pages of Argentina's wine body read through search do not agree whether the law was presented or passed that day, and one records a first Malbec vineyard in Mendoza only in 1865.

Michel Aimé Pouget, who died in 1875, is named once, in an explanation, where the fact needs him. The nursery is not called by its Spanish name, Quinta Normal, because the lint reads Quinta and a capital as a producer.
The Uco Valley as the fresher and more scented zone and Luján de Cuyo as the rounder and darker stand on the Codex's own profile and on trade profiles of the two read through search.

The ladder has two rungs: Cahors, the Loire and Patagonia moderate, Mendoza and Salta warm, as the Court's grid reads Mendoza. Lavender stands beside violet on tasting notes of Uco Valley wines; a checker may prefer violet alone.
The parentage, Prunelard and Magdeleine Noire des Charentes, was confirmed and left out for room. No Creole dish is given: none of the seven suits this grape better than the grill.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.
